html:
A beginners' textbook of Roman private law, written around 161 by a jurist known only as Gaius. It is the only work of classical Roman law that survives nearly whole.

Gaius split the law into three parts, set out in four books: persons (who has what legal status), things (property, inheritance and obligations) and actions (how to go to court). The plan was simple and it lasted. In 533 Justinian's lawyers built their own Institutes on it, as part of the Corpus Juris Civilis, and through that book it shaped how law was taught in Europe for centuries. The same layout still shows in civil codes such as the Napoleonic Code.

The original text was thought lost until 1816, when the historian Barthold Georg Niebuhr found it in Verona, under later writing on a reused parchment.
sum: A beginners' textbook of Roman private law, written around 161 by a jurist known only as Gaius. It is the only work of classical Roman law that survives nearly whole.
